Slides (black), the doctor's notes (green) and every gift (red). Aldughaither's summaries have no oesophagus chapter, so there is no grey section here.

  • Includes: GERD and hiatus hernia · oesophageal motility disorder · oesophageal diverticulum · benign oesophageal tumours · malignant oesophageal tumours · Barrett's oesophagus · oesophageal perforation · caustic injury.

Not required for the exam (the doctor): asphyxia, oesophageal perforation and caustic injury were explicitly excluded; achalasia subtypes (I–III) and exact chemotherapy regimens/trials don't need memorizing. Perforation questions did appear in older exams — they are kept at the end.

The gold-standard test map

For every oesophageal disease, know the gold-standard test — not just the first test you'd order.
DiseaseGold standard / test of choiceNote
GERDpH studyEGD usually first, but a normal EGD does not exclude GERD
AchalasiaManometryA muscle-function disease → a function test
Zenker diverticulumBarium oesophagogramManometry not needed (hard to position at the UES)
Barrett oesophagusEGD + biopsySalmon-coloured mucosa alone is never the diagnosis
LeiomyomaEUSTypical EUS may make biopsy unnecessary
Oesophageal cancerEGD + biopsyThen EUS/CT/PET for staging (EUS → T and N)

GERD & hiatus hernia

  • The LES has the primary role of preventing reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus. GERD may occur when the pressure of the distal high-pressure zone is too low.
  • Reflux = content moves from the high-pressure abdomen to the low/negative-pressure chest (suction) once the LES fails. The refluxate is not only acid — alkaline contents, bile, pepsin, enzymes, food (why PPIs don't fix everything).
  • GERD is often associated with a hiatal hernia — most common is type I (sliding). Types II and III = para-oesophageal hernias (may be associated with GERD). Type IV = another organ herniated into the chest (spleen, colon).
TypeNameGE junctionWhat herniates
ISlidingAbove the diaphragmThe GEJ itself slides up
IITrue para-oesophagealStays below the diaphragmStomach (usually the fundus) alongside the oesophagus
IIIMixed (I + II)Above the diaphragmGEJ + part of the stomach
IVComplexVariableAnother organ — omentum, colon, pancreas, spleen
  • Type IV hiatus hernia → a structure other than stomach (omentum, colon, small bowel). 438
  • Hiatus hernia ≠ GERD. GERD can occur without a hernia; a type II hernia with a competent LES may cause epigastric pain and vomiting without reflux.
  • Definition: symptoms OR mucosal damage from abnormal reflux of gastric contents; often chronic and relapsing; complications may appear in patients without typical symptoms.

Clinical presentation

  • Classic: heartburn, regurgitation, aggravated by change of position, prompt relief by antacid.
  • Overweight 45-year-old with chest discomfort and heartburn, worse with smoking and stress, normal exam → GERD. 436
Extra-oesophageal — pulmonaryENTOther
Asthma, aspiration pneumonia, chronic bronchitis, pulmonary fibrosisHoarseness, laryngitis, pharyngitis, chronic cough, globus, dysphonia, sinusitis, subglottic stenosis, laryngeal cancerChest pain, dental erosion
  • Complicated GERD: dysphagia (food sticks), odynophagia (retrosternal pain on swallowing), GI bleed (haematemesis/melena).
SymptomThink of (doctor)
DysphagiaPeptic stricture or oesophageal cancer
OdynophagiaSevere oesophagitis or oesophageal ulcer
Upper GI bleedingSevere oesophagitis or oesophageal ulcer
Exam trap: peptic STRICTURE is caused by reflux (oesophageal); peptic ULCER is gastric/duodenal, not caused by reflux (H. pylori). They can coexist; one doesn't cause the other.

Diagnostic tests

  • Barium swallow · endoscopy · ambulatory pH monitoring · oesophageal manometry.
TestRole (doctor)
Barium swallowStructural (large hiatus hernia); normal in ~60% of GERD — poor at excluding it
EGDOften first; shows consequences (stricture, oesophagitis B–D, Barrett). Normal EGD doesn't exclude GERD
pH study ★Gold standard — acidic and non-acidic reflux; useful when EGD is normal
ManometryMotility/LES pressure; not for diagnosing GERD — when another motility disorder is suspected

Treatment

  • Lifestyle: elevate the head of the bed 4–6 inches; don't eat within 2–3 h of bedtime; lose weight; stop smoking; smaller, more frequent meals; avoid fatty/fried food, peppermint, chocolate, alcohol, fizzy drinks, coffee and tea; OTC medication prn.
  • Acid suppression: PPIs (omeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole); H2RAs (cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine, nizatidine).
  • Indications for anti-reflux surgery: failed medical management · opt for surgery despite successful medical treatment (age, cost, lifestyle) · complications of GERD (Barrett's; grade III/IV oesophagitis) · complications of a large hiatal hernia (bleeding, dysphagia) · "atypical" symptoms (asthma, hoarseness, cough, chest pain, aspiration) with reflux documented on 24-h pH monitoring.
  • Surgery is an individualized decision: a young PPI-responder unwilling to take lifelong medication is a good candidate; an elderly patient satisfied on PPI may not need surgery.
  • Endoscopic GERD therapy: radiofrequency to the LES (Stretta); suture plication of the cardia; submucosal implantation of inert material (Enteryx); TIF — transoral incisionless fundoplication.
  • TIF is done endoscopically by gastroenterologists; needs specific anatomy; benefits selected patients.
  • Surgical fundoplication: partial (Dor, Toupet) vs complete (Nissen).

Laparoscopic port sites; Nissen fundoplication (before, sutures, after)

Completed wrap at laparoscopy; wrap calibrated over a 60-French bougie (2.5–3 cm, 2–5 sutures)

WrapConfiguration
NissenComplete 360°
ToupetPosterior partial
DorAnterior partial
  • Almost always laparoscopic/robotic. Both partial and complete wraps control reflux well; the doctor favours a partial wrap (less post-op dysphagia).
  • To mobilise the fundus for a tension-free Nissen, ligate the short gastric arteries (branches of the splenic artery). 442
  • Severe reflux after sleeve gastrectomy with BMI 40 → Roux-en-Y bypass (treats GERD + weight). 439 ×3

Achalasia

  • Uncommon oesophageal motility disorder — degeneration of the myenteric neurons that innervate the LES and oesophageal body.
  • Possible pathogenesis: hereditary, degenerative, autoimmune, infectious. Incidence 0.5/100,000; prevalence 1/10,000; ages 20–50, equal sex distribution.
  • The commonest oesophageal dysmotility disorder. Loss of inhibitory neurons → persistently contracted LES → hypertrophy + fibrosis → obstruction. Infectious cause includes Chagas disease. Symptoms often start in the 20s–early 30s.

Clinical features

  • Dysphagia to solids AND liquids — most common (> 90%).
  • Regurgitation of food or saliva — second (~60%).
  • Chest pain; weight loss (end stage); heartburn (irritation by retained food/fermentation); pulmonary symptoms (nocturnal regurgitation → cough, aspiration); adaptive mechanisms.
Dysphagia to solids AND liquids = motility (achalasia); solids first → then liquids = mechanical obstruction (cancer, stricture).
  • Dysphagia of achalasia → to solids and liquids. 439
  • Regurgitation here is stagnant oesophageal food, not gastric reflux. Trap: achalasia can be mislabelled as GERD — don't hand out 6 weeks of PPI without a diagnosis in persistent daily symptoms.

Diagnosis

  • CXR: may show an air-fluid level (widened mediastinum).
  • Barium: dilated oesophagus ± air-fluid level; classic gradual smooth tapering — "bird's beak".
  • Endoscopy: normal in 50%; primary role → rule out pseudoachalasia (malignancy); dilated body with retained food, cobblestone retention oesophagitis; LES tonically closed but the scope passes.

Barium swallow — bird's-beak tapering; massively dilated (sigmoid) oesophagus

  • Manometry has the highest sensitivity: aperistalsis of the distal body · incomplete/absent LES relaxation · hypertensive LES. Manometric variants: type 1, 2, 3.
Manometry = gold standard (the doctor: a muscle-function disease is diagnosed by a function test). Barium shows the bird's beak but doesn't make the diagnosis.
  • Peristalsis ≠ contraction: type III has spastic contractions but still no normal peristalsis — don't write "no contractions".
  • Endoscopy: the scope meets resistance at the LES then passes with a "pop"; cancer gives persistent irregular obstruction. Smooth narrowing = benign; mucosal irregularity = malignancy.
  • Suspected achalasia — confirmatory test → manometry. 437
  • 30-year-old, intermittent dysphagia for 5 years, dilated oesophagus with a tight LES → manometry shows high LES pressure. 437 ×6

Treatment

  • Goal: reduce LES basal pressure; the primary desired outcome is relief of dysphagia.
  • Medical (nitrates; calcium-channel blockers — better tolerated, 30% side effects: oedema, hypotension, headache): inconvenient, modestly effective — for patients awaiting or unfit for invasive treatment.
  • Botulinum toxin: response 78% at 1 month → 58% at 6 months → 49% at 12 months → for non-candidates for invasive treatment.
  • Pneumatic dilation: ruptures LES muscle fibres keeping the mucosa intact; initial response 70%; relapse 6%/year; perforation 2–5%; heartburn 5%; best for older women.
  • POEM — per-oral endoscopic myotomy.
  • Surgical therapy: success > 90%; acid exposure is a known complication; some dysphagia persists (peristaltic dysfunction).
  • Oesophagomyotomy: reduce LES pressure enough for gravity drainage and maintain reflux control; open or MIS (VATS/laparoscopy — laparoscopy has shorter stay, better dysphagia relief, less heartburn). Anterior myotomy at 11 o'clock: 6 cm up the oesophagus (or to the inferior pulmonary ligament), 2–2.5 cm onto the stomach.
  • Achalasia can't be cured (neurons are lost) — all treatment is palliative. Botox lasts 3–4 months. Dilation ≈ myotomy for the first 2 years. POEM → symptomatic GERD in ~40% (PPI doesn't stop non-acid reflux).
Doctor's gold standard: laparoscopic Heller myotomy + PARTIAL fundoplication (prefers Dor — weaker, covers the myotomy). Never a complete wrap after myotomy → outflow obstruction.
  • New dysphagia years after myotomy: recurrent achalasia, reconnection of fibres, reflux adenocarcinoma, or SCC from longstanding achalasia.

Complications

  • From functional obstruction: malnutrition, aspiration. Secondary: epiphrenic diverticula and oesophageal cancer — mostly squamous cell carcinoma (prevalence ~3%).

Oesophageal diverticula

  • Most are due to a primary motor disturbance or an abnormality of the UES or LES. Three common sites: pharyngo-oesophageal (Zenker's), parabronchial (mid-oesophageal), epiphrenic.
  • True = all layers (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis). False = mucosa + submucosa only.
  • Pulsion = false, from raised intraluminal pressure (motility disorders). Zenker's and epiphrenic = false, pulsion. Traction = true, from inflamed mediastinal lymph nodes adhering to the oesophagus.
Mnemonic TNT — True = Traction (middle); Zenker (upper) and epiphrenic (lower) = false pulsion.
LocationNameTypeMechanism
UpperZenkerFalse — pulsionHypertonic cricopharyngeus/UES
MiddleTractionTrue — tractionAdjacent inflammation/lymph node pulling
LowerEpiphrenicFalse — pulsionAchalasia/hypertensive LES
  • True diverticulum → involves all layers of the oesophagus. 438
  • Zenker's diverticulum is a false diverticulum. 439

Zenker's diverticulum

  • Most common oesophageal diverticulum; older patients (7th decade); herniates through Killian's triangle — between the oblique thyropharyngeus and the horizontal cricopharyngeus fibres.
  • Symptoms: sticking in the throat; nagging cough, excessive salivation, intermittent dysphagia; as it enlarges → regurgitation of foul-smelling undigested food; halitosis, voice change, retrosternal pain, respiratory infections.
  • Most serious complication: aspiration pneumonia or lung abscess.
  • Diagnosis: barium oesophagram — neither manometry nor endoscopy is needed.

Zenker's diverticulum on barium swallow

  • Treatment: surgical or endoscopic repair is the gold standard.
  • Endoscopy is not absolutely contraindicated — never push against resistance; it can exclude malignancy (stasis → SCC risk) and look for Barrett.
Cricopharyngeal myotomy is the essential step (without it → recurrence or leak). Diverticulectomy is optional — a pouch ≤ 2 cm may need myotomy alone.
  • 80-year-old with Zenker's — most likely symptom → halitosis. 436
  • 65-year-old: dysphagia to solids, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis → confirm with barium swallow. 441

Barrett's oesophagus

  • Intestinal columnar epithelium (goblet cells) replaces the stratified squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus; chronic reflux injures the squamous lining and promotes columnar metaplasia.
  • Metaplastic cells resist reflux injury but are more prone to malignancy; 10% of GERD patients develop Barrett's; 40-fold increased risk of oesophageal carcinoma.
  • Progression: metaplasia → low-grade → high-grade dysplasia → cancer.
  • 70% are men aged 55–63; men have a 15-fold higher incidence of adenocarcinoma.
Three key words: metaplasia · intestinal · goblet cells. Barrett is metaplasia, not dysplasia.
  • Barrett's oesophagus is associated with → intestinal metaplasia. 439
  • Barrett's predisposes to → adenocarcinoma. 437
  • Many are asymptomatic; most present with GERD symptoms; also recurrent respiratory infections, adult asthma.
  • Warning: reflux symptoms may improve or disappear because metaplastic mucosa is acid-resistant — concerning, not reassuring. More common in obese patients around their 50s.
  • Diagnosis: endoscopy + pathology — any visible columnar segment in the oesophagus with intestinal metaplasia on biopsy.

Barrett's oesophagus — salmon-coloured tongues above the Z-line

  • Salmon-coloured mucosa only raises suspicion (severe oesophagitis can mimic it) — biopsy must show goblet cells.
  • Treatment: surveillance endoscopy in all patients + treat reflux.
  • Manage: treat GERD (PPI or anti-reflux surgery) + surveillance EGD with biopsy every 3–4 years (the doctor).
  • Severe oesophagitis with Barrett's on biopsy → keyed fundoplication (control the reflux; another version keyed PPI + endoscopic surveillance). 438 ×8

Benign oesophageal tumours

  • Rare (< 1%); mucosal vs extramucosal (intramural). 60% leiomyomas, 20% cysts, 5% polyps.

Leiomyoma

  • 60% of benign tumours; men slightly > women; 4th–5th decades; distal two thirds > 80%; usually solitary, intramural; malignant transformation rare.
  • Many asymptomatic; dysphagia and pain most common; CXR unhelpful; characteristic barium appearance (smooth filling defect).

Leiomyoma — smooth filling defect on barium; CT appearance

  • Endoscopy: extrinsic compression with intact mucosa. EUS: hypoechoic mass in the submucosa/muscularis propria.
  • Treatment: observe < 2 cm asymptomatic; most → surgical enucleation (thoracotomy/VATS/robotic); mortality < 2%, dysphagia relief ~100%.
  • EUS = test of choice (typical appearance may make biopsy unnecessary). Enucleation = open the muscle and shell it out; no wide margins needed.

Carcinoma of the oesophagus

  • Fastest-growing cancer in Western countries; SCC and adenocarcinoma.
  • SCC: from native squamous mucosa — upper and middle third 70%.
  • SCC risk factors: smoking and alcohol (5-fold combined), nitrosamines (pickled/smoked food), hot liquids, caustic ingestion, achalasia, bulimia, tylosis (autosomal dominant), Plummer–Vinson, radiation, diverticula.
  • Adenocarcinoma now ~70% in the West — rising GERD, Western diet, more acid suppression; caffeine, fat, acidic/spicy food lower LES tone; Barrett's → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma.
  • 5-year survival: up to 70% with polypoid lesions, as poor as 15% when advanced.
Achalasia → squamous cell carcinoma. GERD / Barrett → adenocarcinoma.
  • GERD and achalasia cause, respectively → adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. 438
  • All predispose to oesophageal cancer except → oesophageal cyst (achalasia, Plummer–Vinson, Barrett's and corrosives do). 428 ×4 428 ×2
  • Barrett's — the false statement → "resected in the metaplasia phase" (metaplasia is surveyed; it predisposes to cancer). 426
  • All are benign oesophageal tumours except → leiomyosarcoma. 426

Symptoms

  • Early → asymptomatic or GERD-like. Most present with dysphagia and weight loss; the oesophagus is distensible — two thirds of the lumen is obstructed before dysphagia.
  • Ominous signs: choking, coughing, aspiration from a tracheo-oesophageal fistula; hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion; metastases to liver, bone, lung.
  • Respiratory symptoms: 1. TE fistula (tracheal invasion) · 2. RLN palsy → aspiration · 3. distal obstruction → regurgitation → aspiration.
  • Early oesophageal cancer — most likely presenting symptom → dysphagia. 436 ×2
  • 60-year-old smoker/drinker, dysphagia solids → then liquids, weight loss → oesophageal cancer. 442

Diagnosis & staging

  • Barium oesophagram for any patient with dysphagia — separates intraluminal vs intramural, intrinsic vs extrinsic; classic apple-core lesion; not specific for cancer but a good first test.

Oesophageal carcinoma on barium — irregular stricture; apple-core lesion

  • Diagnosis is made best by endoscopic biopsy; the operating surgeon must do the endoscopy before resection.

Oesophageal cancer at endoscopy — polypoid and ulcerated tumours

Squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma at endoscopy

  • Suspected oesophageal cancer — best way to reach the diagnosis → endoscopy and biopsy. 439 ×6
  • CT chest/abdomen: tumour length, wall thickness, nodes, liver/lung mets. PET: primary, nodes, distant — slightly better than CT.
  • EUS is the most critical component of staging — guides therapy; biopsies of the mass and paratracheal, subcarinal, para-oesophageal, coeliac nodes.
  • TNM (stages 1–4) determines treatment and prognosis.
Barium appearanceSuspectNext test
Smooth bird's beak / rat-tailAchalasiaManometry
Apple-core / irregularCancerEGD + biopsy
  • T stage = depth of wall layers involved (not size); N = regional nodes.

Treatment

  • Chemotherapy (FLOT, MAGIC) · radiation · chemoradiotherapy (CROSS) · surgical resection: transhiatal, Ivor Lewis, McKeown; open vs MIS (VATS, laparoscopy, robotic).
  • Usually multimodal; upfront surgery only for selected very early disease. FLOT/MAGIC — perioperative chemo (adenocarcinoma); CROSS — chemoradiotherapy then surgery (especially SCC).
OesophagectomyIncisionsAnastomosis
TranshiatalAbdomen + left neck (blunt thoracic dissection, no thoracotomy)Neck
Ivor LewisAbdomen + right chestChest
McKeownAbdomen + right chest + left neckNeck — the doctor's preferred
  • McKeown: more exposure and resection, thoracic dissection under vision, extensive lymphadenectomy, and a neck leak is easier to manage than an intrathoracic one. The stomach is made into a tubular conduit.
  • 75-year-old, stage 3 cancer with heart failure → palliative therapy. 436 ×6
  • Palliation of oesophageal cancer — the keyed "except" → high-beam radiotherapy is very effective (fragmented recall). 426
  • Malnourished man with lower oesophageal carcinoma before surgery → keyed central parenteral nutrition (other versions: gastrostomy feeding — the gut can still be used). 431 ×4
  • After oesophagectomy, drain output rises and turns milky white after oral intake → thoracic duct injury (chylothorax). 439 ×2

From past exams — perforation & bleeding

Added explanationThese topics were not on the slides (perforation was excluded by the doctor; varices belong to portal hypertension) but they appeared in past exams.
  • Alcoholic, violent repeated vomiting → haematemesis + significant chest pain → Boerhaave's syndrome 434 ×3; associated finding (in shock) → subcutaneous emphysema. 431
  • Pneumomediastinum with a contained oesophageal leak, stable → NPO + IV antibiotics (conservative). 441
  • Retching after heavy drinking → haematemesis, no liver disease → Mallory–Weiss tear. 442 ×5
  • Alcoholic with haematemesis, splenomegaly and ascites → oesophageal varices. 429
  • Variceal bleeding with splenomegaly but normal portal vein and liver → left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension (splenic vein thrombosis). 439
  • Cirrhotic with variceal bleeding, after resuscitation → octreotide 437 ×7; IV drug shown to reduce mortality → ceftriaxone (antibiotic prophylaxis). 438 ×6
  • Bleeding varices at endoscopy → most effective → endoscopic sclerotherapy (band ligation preferred today) 439 ×4; varices can be treated by all except → electrotherapy. 426
  • Bleeding varices failing endoscopic therapy, BP 80/40, HR 160 → Minnesota (balloon) tube as a bridge (then TIPS). 426
  • Bleeding varices — all are part of management except → immediate laparotomy. 426
  • Newly diagnosed cirrhosis with varices — prevent the first bleed → propranolol (non-selective β-blocker). 437 ×3
